name: Temporal Input Conditioning
text:
# Temporal Input Conditioning

Also called: Time-conditioned rendering, Dynamic scene parameterization

## Overview
Temporal Input Conditioning parameterizes scene attributes—such as position, [rotation](#19376-rotation.md), opacity, density, or color—as explicit functions of time $t$ to enable novel view synthesis for dynamic scenes [G]. It addresses the challenge of modeling non-rigid motion and temporal evolution from monocular or sparse multi-view inputs without requiring ground-truth geometry or dense multi-view stereo data at every instant [S1]. It sets itself apart from naive time-extended NeRFs by decomposing the representation into static canonical geometry and time-varying deformation fields, or by conditioning radiance fields directly on time, thereby exploiting temporal redundancy that direct 6D mappings fail to capture [S1]. Unlike [DaReNeRF](13782-darenerf.md), which focuses on direction-aware wavelet decompositions, this family establishes the foundational canonical-space and time-conditioning paradigms for [dynamic neural rendering](#9265-dynamic-and-temporal-modeling.md) [G].

## Shared principles
Builds on [Dynamic and Temporal Modeling](9265-dynamic-and-temporal-modeling.md).

## Subtopics

### [D-NeRF](8660-d-nerf.md)
D-NeRF synthesizes novel views at arbitrary time instances for dynamic scenes with complex non-rigid geometries, optimizing a deformable volumetric function from a sparse set of monocular input images. It sets itself apart from naive time-extended NeRFs by decomposing the representation into a static canonical space and a learned deformation field, thereby exploiting temporal redundancy that direct 6D mappings fail to capture. Unlike [DaReNeRF](13782-darenerf.md), which focuses on specific deformation regularizations, D-NeRF establishes the foundational canonical-space paradigm for dynamic neural rendering [G].

### [DaReNeRF](13782-darenerf.md)
DaReNeRF is a method for novel view synthesis of dynamic scenes that employs a direction-aware representation to capture scene dynamics from six distinct orientations. It addresses the shift variance and direction ambiguity (checkerboard artifacts) inherent in traditional 2D Discrete [Wavelet Transforms](#2285-wavelet-transform.md) (DWT) by utilizing the [Dual-Tree Complex Wavelet Transform](#12543-dual-tree-complex-wavelet-transform.md) (DTCWT). Unlike standard plane-based decompositions, DaReNeRF models features from six different directions to eliminate ghosting artifacts around moving objects.

### Time-dependent NeRF
A [NeRF](#1185-nerf-neural-radiance-fields.md) variant that represents scene geometry and appearance at each specific time step $t$, trained using neighboring frames around time $t$, to capture local scene geometry and motion [S1]. It represents scene appearance using a mapping function $c = \phi_c(x, d)$ taking point $x \in \mathbb{R}^3$ and viewing direction $d \in \mathbb{R}^2$ to predict color $c \in \mathbb{R}^3$, and scene geometry via $s = \phi_g(x)$ mapping a 3D point to a signed distance value $s \in \mathbb{R}$ [S1]. For a camera ray $r(h) = o + hd$, it samples $K$ 3D points and uses the time-dependent NeRF to compute [SDF](#1466-signed-distance-fields-sdf.md) flows, which constrain the learning of continuous camera motion via the linear relationship between SDF flow and scene flow [S1]. Density is converted from signed distance $s_i$ using $\sigma_i = \max((\Phi(s_i) - \Phi(s_{i+1}))/\Phi(s_i), 0)$, where $\Phi(s) = 1/(1+e^{1-\gamma s})$ and $\gamma$ is learnable [S1]. Pixel color is rendered via $\hat{C}(r) = \sum_{i=1}^K L_i \sigma_i c_i$, with $L_i = \prod_{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \sigma_j)$ [S1].

### MVControl
Extends ControlNet to the 3D generation task [S2, unofficial]. It allows extra conditioning inputs like edge, depth, normal, and scribbles to be fed into existing multi-view generation models [S2, unofficial].

## Background
The concept of temporal input conditioning in [neural rendering](#6800-neural-rendering.md) originated with D-NeRF, which introduced the canonical space paradigm for dynamic scenes [S1]. This approach allows for the [decomposition](#7254-decomposition.md) of dynamic scenes into static geometry and time-varying deformations, addressing the limitations of direct 6D mappings [S1]. Subsequent works like DaReNeRF have refined this by introducing direction-aware representations to mitigate artifacts such as shift variance and checkerboard effects [S1]. More recent developments, such as the time-dependent NeRF, integrate these concepts with continuous camera motion optimization, using local temporal neighborhoods to constrain SDF flows and improve pose estimation [S1].

## Sources
[S1] Joint Optimization of Neural Radiance Fields and Continuous Camera Motion from a Monocular Video, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52734.2025.01071, fetched 2026-10-26
